EU Directive 2001/83/EC Due to increased availability and use of medicinal products and vaccines, including medical devices, by the population for the management and control of diseases in Sierra Leone there is the need to monitor quality and safety of these products as part of a functioning pharmacovigilance (PV) system.

Guideline on good pharmacovigilance practices (GVP) Module VI – Collection, management and submission of suspected adverse reactions to medicinal products (Rev 2) Detecting and monitoring adverse reactions (ARs) of medicinal products and devices, also known as Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs), and Adverse Events Following Immunisation (AEFIs) are one main part of securing health of the population. In accordance with Act, the Pharmacy Board of Sierra Leone, (hereafter referred to as PBSL), functions as the National Pharmacovigilance Centre (NPC). The regulation of a medicinal product and device in Sierra Leone is governed by the provisions and requirements of the Act by which PBSL was established as the regulatory body for medicinal products and devices. The PBSL is mandated to ensure that evidence of existing and new adverse events, interactions and information about pharmacovigilance of

candidates.statement: This guideline for ADRs is intended for, guidance to all PV stakeholders in Sierra Leone, including but not limited to patients, healthcare professionals (HCPs), public health programmes, hospitals/clinics, marketing authorization holders (MAHs), manufacturers, distributors, importers and exporters of medicinal products and vaccines including medical devices. The guidance herein is also provided to help the PBSL in the continuous monitoring of the safety, efficacy, and benefit to risk balance of medicinal products granted marketing authorization (MA) in Sierra Leone. All stakeholders in PV in Sierra Leone are required to strictly adhere to this guideline. It describes who can report suspected cases of ADRs to the NPC, how to report and the content of the report. It explains what happens after reports are sent and underlines the benefits of a strong pharmacovigilance system. PBSL through the Drug Safety Monitoring Programme aims to ensure optimal safety of medicinal products and devices by detecting, assessing and preventing drug related adverse events/reactions.

PBSL may rely on methods, tools, common processes, standards and templates developed for the safety monitoring by other national and international organisations and implement changes to the existing processes accordingly, if necessary. candidates.statement: Web site: www.pharmacyboard.gov.sl The effectiveness of safety monitoring of medicinal products including vaccines and medical devices in Sierra Leone by PBSL is directly dependent on the active participation of the whole population of Sierra Leone. The importance of healthcare professionals should be acknowledged. All healthcare providers (physicians, pharmacists, dentists and others) should report adverse reactions to PBSL as part of their professional responsibility, also in case of doubts about causality. Also, consumers should report suspected adverse reactions to their HCPs or directly to PBSL. HCPs, MAHs and manufacturers are key stakeholders in the detection and reporting of safety issues of medicinal products and devices marketed in Sierra Leone.
candidates.context: National Pharmacovigilance Centre Pharmacovigilance and Clinical Trials Department Pharmacy Board of Sierra Leone Central Medical Stores Compound, Freetown, Sierra Leone. 2.0 Objective The objective of this guide is to promote early detection of drug safety problems, improve selection and rational use of drugs by HCPs and to reduce medicinal product-/ device-induced morbidity and mortality. Effective PV activity will enable Sierra Leone to develop a good record keeping habit and build a useful safety information database that will improve the quality of health care offered to the patient.

candidates.statement: 4.0 Requirements and general principles of efficient ADR reporting All healthcare professionals (HCPs)/workers, including doctors, dentists, pharmacists, pharmacy technicians, nurses, community health officers, traditional medicine practitioners and other health professional are requested to report all suspected adverse reactions. Consumers should report suspected adverse reactions to their HCPs or directly to PBSL. This should be done without regard to a possible alternative causality or existing lack of information. It applies to all medicinal products and medical devices including orthodox medicines, vaccines, biological products, X-ray contrast media, cosmetics, traditional and herbal remedies, household chemical agents, and nutritional agents. This includes all healthcare institutions such as primary, secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, public health programmes as well as patients/consumers, MAH and manufacturers.

The ICP can be any healthcare professional designated by the facility to perform PV activities with training and experience in PV. If the ICP designated by the facility lacks PV training, the NPC can provide training to enable the person to adequately perform this role.

The Board may provide feedback of evaluation of an ICSR to the reporter after the safety assessment of the submitted report, if it has an implication for further treatment of the patient or leads to regulatory actions. In order to assess the likelihood that the suspected adverse reaction is actually due to the medicinal product, the WHO- UMC and Naranjo have provided a list of causality assessment criteria for deciding the association of the medicine towards the adverse event (Appendix 2).
